newsitem.title: SWEDEN: SWIMMING-AUSTRALIA DAY AT WORLD SHORT-COURSE MEETING.
newsitem.headline: SWIMMING-AUSTRALIA DAY AT WORLD SHORT-COURSE MEETING.

text.p: Australia raced away with three titles and celebrated with China the distinction of setting a world relay record on the opening day of the world short-course swimming championships on Thursday.

Matthew Dunn and Emma Johnson claimed respective gold medals in the men's and women's 400 metres individual medley events, Dunn retaining his title with his rivals way behind and Johnson prevailing in a gritty battle against German European short-course champion Sabine Herbst.
Adrian Radley, Phil Rogers, Geoff Huegill and Michael Klim capped Australia's day with a rousing world record in the men's 4x100 metres medley relay.
They clocked three minutes 30.66 to beat the 3:30.91 set by Radley, Ryan Mitchell, Huegill and Klim in Melbourne on December 22 last year.
"We got off to a very good start and now we've got to sustain it," Australian head coach Don Talbot said.
China closed the evening in the custom-built 25-metre pool in the Scandinavium indoor arena with the second world record of the night.

Wang Luna, Nian Yin, Chen Yan and Shan Ying swam home in 7:51.92 to better the 7:52.45 recorded by Shan, Zhou Guanbin, Le Jingyi and Lu Bin at the inaugural world short-course championships in Palma de Mallorca in December 1993.
The finals got off to a confusing start when Klim was credited on the electronic scoreboard with victory in the opening 100 metres butterfly in a time nearly two seconds inside the world record.

Polish-born Klim was initially given as first in 50.13 seconds ahead of Sweden's Lars Frolander in 51.91 but the result was corrected and the home crowd roared their approval when Frolander was officially declared the winner in a championship record 51.95.
Huegill took the silver in 51.99 and Klim the bronze in 52.02 in a final for which Russian Olympic champion Denis Pankratov failed to qualify.
The Australians protested over the revised result but ultimately realised the original result was wrong, caused by an over-sensitive touch pad at the end of Klim's lane which had to be replaced.

"I'd have been satisfied with the silver medal," Frolander said. "It was quite impossible to say if I finished first or second but it was obvious that it was all wrong on the scoreboard...I feel sorry for Klim for losing the title so abruptly."
China's Liu Limin produced a fierce finishing burst to overhaul Japan's Hitomi Kashima and American Misty Hyman in the women's 200 metres butterfly.
It was the third butterfly gold in three world short-course championships for Liu, who won the 200 in 1993 and the 100 in 1995.
But Chinese compatriot Le Jingyi conceded the 100 freestyle title she won, along with the 50 freestyle, at both the preceding world short-course championships.

Olympic and world long-course champion Le had to settle for the bronze in 53.72 behind American Jenny Thompson (53.46) and German European short-course champion Sandra Voelker, who set a cracking early pace and finished second in 53.50.

"This is my first short-course meet ever and I'm actually pretty surprised that I won," Thompson, a relay gold medallist at the last two Olympics, said. "I thought I was fading at the end. I didn't think I had it until I saw the scoreboard."
Gustavo Borges retained the 200 metres freestyle title he won on home territory in a pool on Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana Beach in December 1995.
Borges controlled the race throughout and won in 1:45.45 from New Zealand's Trent Bray and Germany's Lars Conrad.
Dunn retained his 400 individual medley crown in style, winning by nearly six seconds and beating his own championship record in 4:06.89.
Way behind, only one-hundredth of a second separated Chinese silver medallist Xie Xuefeng and joint bronze medallists Ron Karnaugh of the U.S. and Christian Keller of Germany.
Seventeen-year-old compatriot Johnson won the women's 400 individual medley in 4:35.18 and then the medley quartet made it three wins in three consecutive races for the Australians.
Australia had to wait until the last day of the 1996 Atlanta Olympics for their first swimming golds, courtesy of Kieren Perkins and Susan O'Neill.
"In the Olympics and other events we got off so bad and then we finished very strongly," Talbot said. "We've got some good events to come but you saw tonight it's very tough."
